items.originalTitle: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
items.summary:
Andrej Karpathy highlights a widening gap in shared understanding of large language model (LLM) capabilities, dividing roughly into four groups: about 6 billion people with little exposure, 1-2 billion casual users of free-tier chatbots, 20 million professionals using advanced LLMs for complex math and coding tasks, and around 5,000 insiders with access to frontier-grade systems driving rapid innovation. This divergence stems from differences in access, use cases, and the scale of problems tackled by these models.
Karpathy explains that most of the general public encounters LLMs as simple chatbots with limited utility, while a small professional segment experiences transformative productivity gains in software development and research. The most advanced users are leveraging LLMs for large-scale projects like software creation, cybersecurity, and scientific discovery, often outpacing human comprehension. This split reflects varying levels of ambition, domain specificity, and system access, creating a sharp funnel of understanding and impact across the global population.

items.title: Sakana AI researchers introduce MASS, a multi-agent self-supervision system enabling recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence in AI models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence
items.summary:
Sakana AI and UC Berkeley researchers have developed Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), a system where a single AI model acts as task executor, workflow optimizer, and evaluator to recursively improve itself using collective intelligence. MASS optimizes multi-agent workflows and distills their collective experience as a self-supervision signal, improving performance on research benchmarks without external verification.

MASS operates by having the model optimize team workflows based on its own evaluations, then retrain itself on the best-performing workflows in a loop. This approach addresses challenges in advancing AI beyond human knowledge, especially for tasks lacking verifiable evaluation criteria, by leveraging the model's own capabilities to guide its improvement. The system aims to enable continual self-learning where the AI is both the optimizer and the optimizee.

items.title: TorrentClaw launches AI-powered torrent site with TrueSpec tool to verify content and detect malware in over six million indexed torrents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Built Torrent Site Looks Inside Downloads to Catch Fakes and Malware
items.summary:
TorrentClaw, a torrent search engine launched in February, uses artificial intelligence to organize and verify torrents, including a feature called TrueSpec that checks if torrents match their descriptions and scans for malware using VirusTotal. The site indexes more than six million torrents from its own DHT crawler and external sources, focusing on films and TV shows.

TrueSpec downloads small portions of torrents to analyze video files and detect deceptive or malicious content, labeling torrents with malware warnings and disabling downloads when threats are found. While the system is not perfect and some false positives occur, it has identified rare malware cases, mostly involving trojan-infected VLC media player copies disguised as popular new releases. TorrentClaw aims to improve torrent security and reliability by automating verification processes that are typically manual or absent on other sites.

items.title: Researchers find AI agents breached 27 online retailers, stealing over 600,000 credit card records for about $25 per company [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: AI agents broke into 27 online retailers for $25 a company
items.summary:
Researchers recovered a server used by an attacker running an AI-driven burglary operation that launched 105 attacks on online shops between September 10 and 15, 2026, breaching at least 27 companies and extracting over 600,000 credit card records from two of them. The AI tools automated vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and data theft with minimal human input, costing roughly $7,000 over four weeks, averaging about $25 per targeted company.

The attack chain exploited known vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, plaintext storage of one-time passcodes, insecure file uploads, and misconfigured permissions, following a 13-step process to gain root access and extract encrypted credit card data. The AI's advantage was its persistence and speed, scanning hundreds of companies overnight and deploying sophisticated skimming scripts that remained hidden by integrating into existing site resources and deployment pipelines.

This case highlights that the AI did not invent new exploits but automated existing attack techniques at scale and low cost, challenging the notion that smaller or less prominent companies are less likely targets. The findings underscore the importance of standard security hardening practices and vigilance against automated, persistent threats.

items.originalTitle: Self-hosting an AI agent environment with OpenCode and shared memory
items.summary:
A new method for self-hosting AI agent environments uses OpenCode combined with shared memory to provide persistent memory and seamless continuity across multiple machines. This approach allows AI agents to interact with local files and maintain context across sessions without relying on proprietary platforms.

The setup involves syncing shared memory via Dropbox to a VPS running OpenCode, with access controlled through Tailscale and strict security boundaries. This configuration supports flexible model and harness choices, manual memory confirmation to reduce conflicts, and private access, enabling users to manage AI agents with greater control and scalability.
